preamble: Depalatalization of [dʲ] to plain [d] removes the secondary palatal articulation. The clearest case is Ukrainian, where consonants that were soft before front vowels in Common Slavic / Old East Slavic became hard before /e/ (Ukrainian день [dɛnʲ] 'day' against Russian [dʲenʲ]); Rubach (2005) treats this as an active depalatalization process before [ɛ] in Ukrainian phonology. Other Slavic languages with hard [d] before /e/ (Czech den, Bulgarian ден [dɛn]) are not listed because the earlier palatalized stage could not be verified for them.

examples.from: Proto-Slavic *dьnь 'day', soft [dʲ] before a front vowel (cf. Russian день [dʲenʲ])
examples.note: Ukrainian consonants are hard before /e/; Rubach (2005) analyses a depalatalization process applying before [ɛ] that makes o-fronting opaque.

sources: Rubach, J. (2005). Mid vowel fronting in Ukrainian. Phonology 22(1), 1-36. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0952675705000424
